title: Jeremiah
subtitle: To uproot and tear down, to build and to plant
lead: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah was a priest's son from Anathoth, a village a few miles north of Jerusalem. The LORD's word came to him as a young man in the thirteenth year of King Josiah, 627 BC, and he kept speaking it for some forty years: through Josiah's reform and his death in battle (609), the rise of Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar, the first deportation to Babylon (597), the long siege and the burning of Jerusalem and its Temple (586), and on into Egypt, where a band of refugees took him against his will. His commission sums up his work: he was set over nations and kingdoms "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant" (1:10).

Jeremiah has more words than any other book of the Bible. It is not arranged by date. Poems of judgment and grief stand beside long prose sermons, stories told about the prophet by someone else, letters, oracles against foreign nations, and a set of prayers in which Jeremiah argues bitterly with God, often called his confessions. Chapter 36 tells how the book began: Jeremiah dictated his words to the scribe Baruch, King Jehoiakim cut the scroll up and burned it column by column, and Jeremiah dictated it again with many words added. The book also survives in two editions, the longer Hebrew text that Jewish and most Christian Bibles translate and a shorter Greek one, and copies of both were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Jeremiah's words outlived the city whose fall he announced. His seventy years of exile (25:11–12; 29:10) shaped the hopes of Daniel and of the Jews who came home under Persia (2 Chronicles 36:21–22; Daniel 9:2). His letter told the exiles to seek the welfare of the city where they lived (29:7). His promise of a new covenant written on the heart (31:31–34) is quoted in full in Hebrews 8, and Jesus echoed his charge that the Temple had become "a cave for bandits" (7:11) when he drove the traders out (Matthew 21:13). Jewish tradition makes him the author of Lamentations and of Kings, and his words are read in the synagogue in the weeks before the Ninth of Av, the fast that mourns the Temple.
facts: The book is headed "the words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, from among the priests who lived at Anathoth" (1:1). It says that Jeremiah dictated his messages to the scribe Baruch son of Neriah (36:4, 32), and many of its stories speak of Jeremiah in the third person. The Talmud says that Jeremiah wrote his own book, Kings and Lamentations (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a). Most modern scholars think the book grew from Jeremiah's poetry, prose sermons shaped in the style of Deuteronomy, and stories about him, gathered and edited by his disciples and later scribes (see the authorship section).

Jeremiah was active from 627 BC, Josiah's thirteenth year (1:2), until after the fall of Jerusalem in the summer of 586 BC (some count 587), and his last words were spoken in Egypt (43–44). The book's last event is the release of King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon in 561 BC (52:31). The two editions were probably both complete by the 200s BC.

Jerusalem and Judah in the last forty years of the kingdom: the Temple courts, the palace, the prison yard and the cistern where Jeremiah was held. Then Mizpah under the governor Gedaliah, and Tahpanhes and other towns of Egypt. Assyria was collapsing when the book opens, and Babylon replaced it as master of the region after the battle of Carchemish (605 BC).

Prophecy: oracles in Hebrew poetry (most of 2–20, 30–31 and 46–51), prose sermons (such as 7, 11 and 34), stories about the prophet (26–29, 32–45), symbolic actions, a letter (29), laments and prayers. Chapter 52 is a historical appendix that runs parallel to 2 Kings 24:18–25:30.
Hebrew, with one verse in Aramaic (10:11). The Greek translation was made in Egypt, probably in the 100s BC, from a Hebrew text shorter than the one the Masoretes preserved.
52 chapters, 1,364 verses, about 21,800 Hebrew words: the longest book of the Bible by word count. The Greek edition is about one-seventh shorter.

The Greek lacks about 2,700 words of the Hebrew, and it places the oracles against the nations (Hebrew 46–51) in the middle of the book, after 25:13, in another order. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, two copies (4QJer-b and 4QJer-d) agree with the shorter text and three (4QJer-a, 4QJer-c and 4QJer-e) with the longer. Many scholars, following Emanuel Tov and Pierre-Maurice Bogaert, think the Greek translates an earlier edition of the book, and the Hebrew a later, expanded one; others think the Greek translator or his source shortened it.

4QJer-a from Qumran Cave 4, copied around 200 BC by the usual dating of its handwriting, is one of the oldest of all the scrolls. Six copies in all survive from Qumran (2QJer and 4QJer-a to -e). The Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), the base of this translation, is the oldest complete Hebrew copy.

In printed Hebrew Bibles it is the second of the Latter Prophets, after Isaiah. The Talmud (Bava Batra 14b) lists the prophets as Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and some medieval manuscripts follow that order. In Protestant Bibles it follows Isaiah and comes before Lamentations. Catholic Bibles follow it with Lamentations and Baruch, whose last chapter is the Letter of Jeremiah. Orthodox Bibles, which keep the Greek order, have Jeremiah, Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter of Jeremiah.

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: Reads each oracle and scene against the dates the book gives and the events it names: Josiah's reform (622 BC), his death at Megiddo (609), Carchemish (605), the first deportation (597), the siege and fall of Jerusalem (588–586), Gedaliah's murder and the flight to Egypt. It traces how the events Jeremiah announced turned out, including the seventy years.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book was made: the poetry most scholars give to Jeremiah, the prose sermons in the language of Deuteronomy, the stories about him (often credited to Baruch), and the two editions of the book, the longer Hebrew and the shorter Greek with its different order, which Qumran copies show were both in use. It weighs the Babylonian Chronicle, the Lachish and Arad letters and the seals and bullae of the period.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: How the Targum, the rabbis and the medieval commentators (Rashi, Kimchi, Abravanel) read Jeremiah: the prophet of the destruction read on the Ninth of Av, the author by tradition of Lamentations and of Kings (Bava Batra 15a), and the source of the hope of return and of the new covenant.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: How the New Testament and the church read Jeremiah: the temple sermon in Jesus' cleansing of the temple, Rachel weeping in Matthew 2, the new covenant at the Last Supper and in Hebrews 8, and Jeremiah as a figure of the suffering Christ.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: Reads the promises of return, a righteous Branch from David and a renewed Israel in its land (23:5–8; 30–33) as still waiting for their full fulfillment: in many Christian readings at Christ's return (premillennial and dispensational), and in Jewish hope in the days of the Messiah.

sections.b:
The Plain English Translation is made from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (the Leningrad Codex, AD 1008, with its few Aramaic words), one verse at a time, starting from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew. Verse numbers are the English ones. Where the Greek Jeremiah is much shorter, this site still translates the longer Hebrew, and each important difference is shown as a variant that the reader can switch on.

Each chapter page says which witnesses the writer read directly: the Hebrew text and its marginal readings on the site, the Dead Sea Scrolls through the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcriptions, and the Greek in Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus (with Ziegler's critical text cited as reported by the commentaries). Later translations (the Targum, the Vulgate, the Peshitta) and the medieval Jewish commentators are cited as reported by the sources named in each note.

The divine name is 'the LORD'; a prophecy begins 'The LORD says this' and ends 'the LORD declares'. Where Jeremiah plays on words, the English keeps the play where it can and a note shows the Hebrew.

Anathoth and the priests. Jeremiah came from a priestly family at Anathoth in Benjamin (1:1), a village about three miles north-east of Jerusalem. Many scholars connect it to the line of Abiathar, the priest whom Solomon sent to his fields at Anathoth when he made Zadok sole high priest (1 Kings 2:26–27). This is a guess, not a statement of the text; the book never says it. His own townsmen later plotted against him (11:21).

The kings. The book dates the call to the thirteenth year of Josiah, 627 BC (1:2), and the last event it names in the prophet's own life is after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. In between were Josiah's reform (622) and his death at Megiddo (609), the rise of Babylon and its defeat of Egypt at Carchemish (605), Jehoiakim's rebellion, the first deportation with King Jehoiachin (597), Zedekiah's reign and the second rebellion, the siege, the fall and burning of the city and the Temple (586), Gedaliah's governorship and murder, and the flight of a band of Judeans to Egypt, who took Jeremiah with them (chapters 40–44). The dates here follow the site's 2 Kings: Josiah reigned 640–609 BC, Jehoiakim 609–598, Jehoiachin three months in 598–597 (Jerusalem surrendered in March 597), and Zedekiah 597–586. Some scholars date the fall in 587.

Baruch. Baruch son of Neriah, a scribe, wrote down what the prophet dictated (36:4) and appears at his side in the worst days (32:12–16; 43:3, 6; 45). Two clay seal impressions said to name him have been published; their authenticity is debated, and they are treated where the book reaches them.

The book is a collection, not a chronicle. It mixes poems of judgment and grief, prose sermons in a style close to Deuteronomy, stories about Jeremiah told by someone else, symbolic acts, a letter, prayers, oracles against foreign nations, and a historical appendix. Chapter 36 shows how at least part of it began: a scroll dictated in 605 BC, burned, and written again with additions. The whole is not in date order, and the later editors' headings do not always agree with the order of the chapters. See the authorship section for the theories of Duhm, Mowinckel, Nicholson, Thiel, Carroll and the defenders of Jeremiah's and Baruch's own part.

The poems of 2–6, set in this part, are widely held to be among the oldest. They are spoken for the most part in the voice of the LORD, sometimes in the prophet's own cry (4:19–21; 6:10–11) and sometimes in the voice of the people (3:22–25).

The Greek Jeremiah (the Septuagint, translated in Egypt about the 100s BC) differs from the Hebrew in two ways. It is shorter, by roughly 2,700 words, most of it single words and phrases such as titles and 'the LORD declares', but also whole passages (for example 10:6–8, 10; 33:14–26; 39:4–13; 51:44–49). And the oracles against the nations, which the Hebrew puts at the end (46–51), stand in the Greek after 25:13, in a different order.

At Qumran, 4QJer-b and 4QJer-d agree with the short text; 4QJer-a, 4QJer-c and 4QJer-e agree with the longer. On this evidence the shorter form existed in Hebrew before the Greek was made, which is why Tov and Bogaert hold that the Greek translates an earlier edition. A minority, citing the translator's habits in other books, holds that the Greek is an abridgment. The variants in each part show where this affects the reading.

Jeremiah is a prophet of destruction and consolation. In many synagogues the first chapters (1:1–2:3 and 2:4–28 with 3:4, in the Ashkenazi custom) are the haftarot of the first two of the three Sabbaths of rebuke before the Ninth of Av, the fast for the destruction of the First and Second Temples; 8:13–9:23 is the haftarah of the morning service on the Ninth of Av itself. The Talmud lists Jeremiah among the prophets first in order (Bava Batra 14b) and says he wrote Kings and Lamentations (Bava Batra 15a). The medieval commentators Rashi, Kimchi (Radak) and Abravanel read the book chiefly as a history of the last kings, with the promises of return and the new covenant looking ahead to the days of the Messiah.

sections.h: Jeremiah in the New Testament and the church
sections.b:
The New Testament quotes Jeremiah often. Jesus' words at the Temple, 'you have made it a den of robbers', echo Jeremiah 7:11, 'a cave for bandits' (Matthew 21:13; Mark 11:17; Luke 19:46). Matthew sees Rachel weeping for her children (31:15) in Herod's killing of the boys at Bethlehem (Matthew 2:17–18), and attributes a quotation about the potter's field to Jeremiah (Matthew 27:9–10), a text that blends Zechariah 11:12–13 with Jeremiah 18:2–3 and 32:6–15. Jesus is said by some in the crowd to be Jeremiah come back (Matthew 16:14). At the Last Supper he speaks of the cup of the new covenant (Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25), and Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34 in full (Hebrews 8:8–12; 10:16–17). Paul uses 9:23–24 in 'Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord' (1 Corinthians 1:31; 2 Corinthians 10:17).

The church fathers read the suffering prophet as a pattern of Christ. Origen preached on Jeremiah in Caesarea, and Jerome, in his last years, began a commentary on Jeremiah (begun about AD 414) that he left unfinished at his death in 420; it stops at chapter 32. At the Reformation Calvin wrote a long commentary on Jeremiah and Lamentations.

Lamentations, five poems on the fall of Jerusalem, is placed after Jeremiah in Christian Bibles and credited to him by the Talmud, though the book itself names no author. Baruch is a short book in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, set in Babylon in the name of Jeremiah's scribe; its last chapter, the Letter of Jeremiah, warns against idols and stands as a separate book in the Greek and Orthodox Bibles. Outside the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles are two more works in the names of Baruch and Jeremiah. 2 Baruch (the Syriac Apocalypse of Baruch, after AD 70) is in no church's Bible. The story called the Paralipomena of Jeremiah or 4 Baruch (about the Babylonian exile and a sleep of sixty-six years) is Scripture only for the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which calls it the Rest of the Words of Baruch. Both are late works, written long after Jeremiah, and neither is part of the book of Jeremiah in any church.

sections.h: How to read the first six chapters
sections.b: Chapters 1–6 are the best-known of the book's early poems and are probably among its oldest. They run in three movements: the call (1), the LORD's lawsuit and the pleading to turn back (2:1–4:4), and the foe from the north (4:5–6:30). The word shuv ('turn, return') is the key: the people have turned away, and the LORD begs them to turn back (3:12–14, 22; 4:1). The reader should ask who the 'foe from the north' is. Babylon was not yet the master of the region in 627 BC, and so some think the poems were first about another invader and were later read as about Babylon (see 1:13–15).

audience.to: Jeremiah first spoke to the people of Judah and Jerusalem between 627 and 586 BC: to crowds at the Temple gates and in its courts, to the kings Jehoiakim and Zedekiah and their officials, to priests and to other prophets, and to the men of his own village. After the city fell he spoke to the survivors at Mizpah and to the Judeans who fled to Egypt, and he wrote to the exiles in Babylon (29). The finished book was read by Jews who had lived through the disaster or grown up after it, in Babylon, in Egypt and in the ruined land of Judah.
audience.why: Before 586 the words were a warning and a summons: Judah had broken its covenant with the LORD, worshiped other gods and wronged the poor, and unless it turned back, a foe from the north would destroy the city and the Temple that the people trusted to protect them. Jeremiah also told kings to submit to Babylon, which made him a traitor in many eyes. After 586 the same words became an explanation and a hope. They told the survivors that the disaster was not the defeat of their God but his judgment, foretold and deserved; that the prophets who had promised peace were liars; and that the LORD who tore down would also build and plant, bring the exiles home after seventy years and make a new covenant with them. Reading the book with both audiences in mind explains why warnings and comfort stand side by side.
views: Jeremiah and Baruch for the generation of the exile

Many scholars, especially conservative ones, think Jeremiah and his scribe Baruch gathered most of the book themselves, beginning with the scroll of 605 BC (36), to warn Judah and then to explain the fall to the exiles; the stories of 26–45 read like the work of an eyewitness close to the prophet (Bright; Thompson; Lundbom, who sees Baruch and his brother Seraiah as the book's first editors).

Many critical scholars think the prose sermons were written or reshaped by later editors in the language of Deuteronomy, to answer the questions of the exiles in Babylon: why had the LORD let Jerusalem fall, and what must they do now? On this view much of the book speaks first to the exile community through Jeremiah's voice (Nicholson; Thiel; Carroll, who thinks little of the book can be traced back to the prophet himself).

Because the shorter Greek edition was translated in Egypt and the longer Hebrew one was completed later, some scholars see the book still being supplemented in the Persian period, perhaps in Babylon or Judah, with additions such as 33:14–26 that answered new questions about David's line and the priests (Tov; Bogaert; Janzen).

authorship: The book itself says that Jeremiah dictated a scroll of his messages to Baruch son of Neriah in 605 BC, that King Jehoiakim burned it, and that Jeremiah dictated it again with many similar words added (36:1–4, 27–32). Jewish tradition gives Jeremiah a large share in the Bible: the Talmud says he wrote his own book, Kings and Lamentations (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 15a). Conservative scholars such as J. A. Thompson and Jack Lundbom accept that the prophet and his scribe stand behind most of the book, and Lundbom sees Baruch and his brother Seraiah as its first editors.
Sources A, B and C (Duhm and Mowinckel)

In 1901 Bernhard Duhm sorted the book into three layers: about sixty poems that he gave to Jeremiah himself, a biography of the prophet that he credited to Baruch (mainly chapters 26–45), and a large body of prose speeches and additions from later writers. Sigmund Mowinckel (1914) named the layers A (the poetry), B (the stories about Jeremiah) and C (the long prose sermons in the style of Deuteronomy), and added a fourth, D, for the oracles of hope in 30–31. This outline is still the starting point for most critical study, though almost every part of it has been challenged.
The prose as the voice of the exile

Ernest Nicholson and Winfried Thiel argued that the C prose is not Jeremiah's own preaching reported by Baruch but the work of editors, writing in the Deuteronomistic style (the language of Deuteronomy, Joshua and Kings), who shaped the book for Judeans in exile and explained to them why Jerusalem fell. Robert Carroll went further and doubted that much of the book can be traced to the prophet at all. Against this, Bright, Holladay and Lundbom point to the many places where the prose has a vocabulary and rhythm of its own and to the poetry's close links with the prose, and conclude that Jeremiah's own preaching lies behind much of it.

The Greek Jeremiah is about one-seventh shorter than the Hebrew and arranges the book differently. Since the Qumran scrolls include copies of both forms (4QJer-b and 4QJer-d with the short text, 4QJer-a and 4QJer-c with the longer), most scholars now hold that the book was published in two editions. Emanuel Tov and Pierre-Maurice Bogaert hold that the Greek translates the earlier edition and that the Hebrew we read is a later, expanded one. A minority holds that the Greek translator, or his Hebrew source, shortened a text like the Masoretic one. Either way, the longer text is the one used in synagogues and in most Bibles, and this site translates it.

reading: A clear, historical commentary from a scholar who defends the prophet's own part in the prose.
A close study of the Hebrew with a full account of the prophet's career and the book's dates.
Jack R. Lundbom, Jeremiah 1–20, 21–36 and 37–52, Anchor Bible 21A–C (1999–2004)
A large commentary strong on the book's rhetoric and on Baruch's part in making it.
Robert P. Carroll, Jeremiah, Old Testament Library (1986)
The main critical commentary that doubts how much goes back to the prophet.
Walter Brueggemann, A Commentary on Jeremiah: Exile and Homecoming (1998)
A theological reading of the book as a response to the loss of the world Israel had known.
Emanuel Tov, 'Some Aspects of the Textual and Literary History of the Book of Jeremiah' (1981)
The article that set out the case that the Greek translates an earlier edition.
prompts: A young man in a plain wool tunic stands on a stony hillside near a small village of flat-roofed houses and olive trees. An enormous hand, drawn in thick ink strokes like a cave painting, reaches down from the top of the picture to touch the young man's lips. Fine lines of script spill out of his mouth and spread across the sky like birds. The edges fade into the rough, cracked texture of an old scroll.
The almond branch and the pot (1:11–14)

Two panels sketched on one weathered parchment. On the left, a bare almond branch with white blossoms, an open eye drawn in the center of one blossom. On the right, a large clay cooking pot tipped to pour away from a fire, its mouth turned toward the north, steam streaming out and a dark line of marching soldiers on the horizon. Soft, uneven ink edges, no hard rectangle.

A spring of clear water gushing from a rock, drawn in blue wash, while beside it people dig rough round pits in dry ground; the plastered cisterns crack and the water drains away. Ancient-manuscript style with a few hieroglyph-like marks along the border.

A watchman on the wall of a hill city blowing a ram's horn; behind him on the northern horizon a dark storm of chariots and horsemen. In the streets villagers run toward the gates with bundles. Charcoal and ochre, loose lines, torn scroll edges.

traditions.q: Are Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah part of the Bible?
views: Yes. The Catechism of the Catholic Church lists Baruch among the books of the Old Testament (120), and the Catholic Bible prints the Letter of Jeremiah as Baruch chapter 6. Catholics call these books deuterocanonical, meaning that the church fixed their place in the canon later than the books of the Hebrew Bible, not that they are lesser.

Yes. The Orthodox churches print Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah (as a separate book) after Jeremiah in the Greek Old Testament, and Baruch is read in worship (Baruch 3:35–4:4 at Vespers on the eve of the Nativity). The Confession of Dositheus (Jerusalem, 1672) takes as Sacred Scripture the books listed by the Synod of Laodicea, whose list has 'Jeremiah, and Baruch, the Lamentations, and the Epistle', and adds seven more books of the Greek Bible. The Orthodox Church in America's Questions and Answers names 'the Prophecy of Baruch' among the books of the longer canon that the Orthodox count as fully part of the Old Testament; it does not name the Letter.

Not as Scripture on a level with the others. Luther's German Bible (Wittenberg, 1545) printed the books outside the Hebrew canon, Baruch among them with the Letter of Jeremiah attached to it, in a separate section headed Apocrypha: books not held equal to Holy Scripture, yet useful and good to read.
No. The Westminster Confession says the books 'commonly called Apocrypha' are not inspired and are not part of the canon, and so are of no authority in the church (1.3).
They may be read 'for example of life and instruction of manners' but not used 'to establish any doctrine' (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 6, 1571).

Yes, and more. R. W. Cowley lists Baruch among the books of the narrower canon of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, counted as equally fully canonical, and in its Bible Baruch follows Jeremiah, with the Letter ('the epistle to the captives') inside a longer book of Jeremiah's lamentations. That book also holds a further work in Baruch's name: the Rest of the Words of Baruch, also called 4 Baruch or the Paralipomena of Jeremiah, a story about the exile and Jeremiah's scribe. The Catholic, other Orthodox and Protestant churches do not count that work as Scripture.
